newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: FEATURE-Zambian economy struggles against the past.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Zambian economy struggles against the past.

text.p: More than three decades after independence, Zambia is battling against the legacy of past policies which made the southern African country one of the poorest in the world.
With a general election due next week, Zambia is in the throes of an ambitious privatisation programme lauded by the World Bank and expects five percent real growth this year.
Yet the ordinary Zambian remains dirt poor.
Average per capita income is about $350 a month, according to the World Bank, and the price of a decent meal in one of Lusaka's restaurants would feed a poor family for a month, aid officials say.
Buildings in Lusaka are dirty, run down and show years of neglect while the city has to cope with a steady influx of rural Zambians seeking work.
Crime is rife and none but the very foolish venture into the city centre at night.
For years, Zambia has relied on copper exports for more than 80 percent of foreign earnings but falling copper prices and an oversupplied world market have steadily reduced its income from the metal.
Much of Zambia's income from metal exports is being used to service the country's huge foreign debt of $6.4 billion.

If that was not enough, international donors suspended aid to President Frederick Chiluba's government in June in protest against constitutional changes which outlawed former Zambian president Kenneth Kaunda from contesting the election, due to be held on November 18.

Analysts said they expected a low voter turnout because Kaunda's United National Independence Party (UNIP) -- the biggest opposition party -- and six other opposition parties were boycotting the election.
They said voter apathy would also play a large role as many Zambians who hailed Chiluba as a saviour when he deposed Kaunda had now turned away from him.
The analysts expected Chiluba's ruling Movement for Multiparty Democracy (MMD) to win but the international community might not recognise the validity of the polls.
Businessmen fear the aid freeze and the boycott could harm the economy.

"There is one big worry that everybody has, the fact that the government and the donors have difficulties. We seem to face a serious funding gap over the next three to six months," Zambia Association of Manufacturers chairman Mark O'Donnell told Reuters.
Finance Minister Ronald Penza said the government was confident of servicing its debt without donor funding but O'Donnell said this would cause chaos.
"If government wants to go it alone then this country goes back to the dark ages," O'Donnell said.
Zambia suffered nearly 30 years of socialism under Kaunda, who ruled for 27 years until he was ousted in a multi-party election five years ago.

After independence from Britain in 1964, Kaunda nationalised about 80 percent of the economy -- including coal mines, breweries and the largest Zambian company, Zambia Consolidated Copper Mines Ltd (ZCCM).
Now the government is selling off its assets to the highest bidder and hopes that the sale of ZCCM will be the boost the country needs.

"The sale of the mines is crucial to this country and we see the Zambian economy blossoming with the (privatisation) of the mine sector," said Charles Mate, general manager of the fledgling Lusaka Stock Exchange, which began trading in February 1994.
Mate has high hopes for the economy once the privatisation process has been completed.
"When you look at the potential for this market to grow once we achieve stability, the potential is certainly enormous," he said.

But outside the new stock exchange building, beggars in rags solicit passersby near ramshackle stalls set up by budding entrepreneurs selling everything from cassettes to second-hand copies of foreign magazines.
The hawkers clutch stacks of the local kwacha currency in their hands and all prices are rounded to the nearest thousand or hundred.
The kwacha has weakened from less than 1,000 to the dollar in January to nearly 1,300 -- and most businessmen expect it to tumble further.
"We don't have coins, they are worthless," commented one resident.
